messages.subject: backwards indexing
parts:
I hope this message finds you well. I am currently working on a population dynamics model using NIMBLE and have encountered several warnings that I would like your guidance on:

  1. Backwards Indexing Warnings:

    • [Warning] Detected backwards indexing in '10:9'. This is likely unintended and will likely not produce valid model code.
    • [Warning] Detected backwards indexing in '12:11'. This is likely unintended and will likely not produce valid model code.
    • [Warning] Detected backwards indexing in '14:13'. This is likely unintended and will likely not produce valid model code.

  2. Non-Constant Indexes Note:

    • [Note] Detected use of non-constant indexes: z[1, 1, 1], z[1, 2, 1], z[1, 3, 1], z[1, 4, 1], z[1, 5, 1], ... For computational efficiency, we recommend specifying these in 'constants'.

I would appreciate any insights into why these errors may be occurring and how I can resolve them. I have attached the relevant model code for your reference.

Thank you for your assistance!

messages.author: dd632bd3bbcdd7e9
messages.subject: Re: backwards indexing
parts:
Dear Nour,
Thanks for posting a question. Did you mean to attach a file?
Backwards indexing sometimes arises when the indices come from (constant) variables, e.g.
for(i in 1:N) {
  for(j in start[i]:end[i]) {
    <some code>
 }
}
then if start[i] > end[i], there will be a backwards indexing warning. That's just a guess of how it can arise.

The non-constant indices warning can arise if those z elements are used as nested indices, e.g.
x[ z[1, 1, 1] ] 
Then nimbleModel checks to see if z was provided via the constants list (as opposed to the data list) and is saying that if the z values are not going to change then it is better to provide them via constants so nimbleModel can take advantage of that. Again that is just a guess at what might trigger the warning.

But anyway please send along your code if those points don't resolve your questions.
Perry
